entities.name: Thomas More
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sir Thomas More (1478–1535) was an English lawyer, statesman, and humanist philosopher who served as Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII before being executed for refusing to acknowledge the king as Supreme Head of the Church of England. His principled stand for papal authority over royal supremacy made him a Catholic martyr, canonized in 1935.

More's 'Utopia' (1516), written in Latin, invented the genre of utopian fiction and introduced the word 'utopia' into European languages. The work described an ideal island society with communal property, religious tolerance, and universal education—a satirical mirror reflecting the injustices of Tudor England.

As Lord Chancellor from 1529, More vigorously prosecuted heretics and opposed the Protestant Reformation. When Henry VIII sought annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon and broke with Rome, More resigned in 1532 and refused to swear the Oath of Supremacy. He was imprisoned in the Tower of London for 15 months.

On the scaffold, More declared himself 'the King's good servant, but God's first.' His friend Erasmus called him 'a man for all seasons.' Robert Bolt's 1960 play popularized this phrase and cemented More's legacy as a man of conscience who chose death over compromise.
